lesson.title: Not Just the Cost, the Whole Path: Path Vector Routing Explained
lesson.summary: Path vector routing extends distance vector routing by advertising the full path to a destination rather than just its cost, which enables simple loop detection and policy based route choices between independently operated networks.
lesson.body:
Link state routing solves the interior routing problem elegantly, but it depends on an assumption that quietly stops holding once you leave a single administratively controlled network: that every router can be trusted to flood truthful information about its links, and that every router is willing to accept the computational and bandwidth cost of learning the entire topology and recomputing shortest paths over it. Across the boundary between two independently operated networks, neither assumption is safe. One organization generally should not get a full, trusted, real time map of another organization's internal topology, and shortest path is not even necessarily what either organization wants, since business relationships and policy often matter more than raw distance. Path vector routing is the routing algorithm family designed for exactly this setting.

Path vector routing is, at its core, a variant of distance vector routing, where a router still only exchanges information with its immediate neighbors rather than flooding to everyone, but instead of advertising only a distance or cost to a destination, it advertises the entire path, the ordered list of intermediate networks used to reach that destination. When a router receives a route advertisement from a neighbor, it can prepend itself to that path before passing the route along to its own neighbors, so a route's advertisement grows a visible trail of everywhere it has been.

This single change fixes two problems at once. First, it solves the looping problem that plagues plain distance vector routing, without needing link state's whole topology flooding: since the full path is visible in every advertisement, a router that receives a route already containing its own identity in the path can simply reject it outright, since accepting that route would create a loop, and no lengthy count to infinity process is needed to discover that the route is bad. Second, and just as important at internet scale, because the actual sequence of networks is visible rather than collapsed into a single number, each router is free to choose a route using its own policy: preferring a path through a business partner, avoiding a path through a network it does not trust or has no agreement with, or overriding a shorter path in favor of a policy preferred but longer one, none of which is expressible in a system that only ever exchanges bare costs. Path vector routing therefore trades away the guarantee of finding a globally shortest path, which link state protocols like OSPF chase within a single network, for the flexibility that independent, mutually distrustful networks actually need when they interconnect.
